comments.author: bryanlarsen

A Lisp, an OO language, a functional language, Prolog, VHDL or Verilog, a Forth, et cetera.   They'll all make you think differently and teach you lessons you will use outside of the family.

comments.author: dabinat
comments.text:
One of the things that I think makes Rust unique is that it acknowledges the possibility of human error. I think it’s also one of the most controversial too: there are certain people who get an ego hit at the insinuation that they ever could have written C code with mistakes.
Instead of hoping you remember to check for NULL, Rust forces you to make a decision on how to handle the possibility of failure. Sure, you can still pick a bad decision (unwrap) but that is at least a specific decision and you can’t forget to do it.
You can take it even further with things like the newtype pattern. If you have lots of numeric IDs (project ID, user ID, etc) you can give them distinct types so you don’t mix them up.
So Rust taught me I can program defensively against my own brain, which sometimes gets tired or lazy or distracted.

comments.author: xeubie
comments.text: Rust enums conflate the tag type with the union type that uses it. These should be separate things. In the example here, you can see that Rust gives no way to represent the tag type `{Human, Cat}`. In Zig there is an enum which is a set of tags, and a union which is backed by that enum and can have fields. It is obviously better to have these as separate concepts rather than conflating them. You often want the kind without the data, and Rust gives you no way to represent it. I'm not sure why I am bothering to rant about this but it's one of my biggest annoyances with the language.

stories.title_en: How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

comments.author: rbartelme
comments.text:
The key requirement here is the client has to trust the proxy's CA. It's a client-side MITM, and the article itself notes pinned apps reject it. QUIC's crypto is fine. HTTP/3 just stopped being a blind spot for corporate TLS-inspection boxes.
It's more interesting to split tunnel designs by where the trust lives:
- ngrok / Cloudflare Tunnel: the edge terminates TLS by design, and your public hostname is ordinary WebPKI. Anyone who controls a visitor's trust store (inspection appliance, malware root cert) can do exactly this, and the provider can see plaintext anyway.
- iroh-style P2P QUIC: there's no CA in the loop. You dial a public key (the EndpointId), and the TLS handshake authenticates raw keys, so it's pinned by construction. Relays forward ciphertext they can't terminate. A rogue root cert gets an attacker nothing; they'd need the peer's secret key.
So "can someone MITM my HTTP/3?" really comes down to "who can add to the set of keys my client trusts?" For WebPKI that's a long list. For key-addressed transports it's nobody: the trusted key is the address you dialed, unless an endpoint's secret key (or the machine itself) is already compromised.

The electricity industry has this notion they call a black start, where they bring the grid online from zero. It's a very difficult operation because you can't start a generator straight into an offline grid otherwise it gets hit with full demand and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment. So they have to start by disconnecting all the loads and then bringing load blocks back in sequence, trying to roughly balance available generation with the size of the next block. In practice black starts are extremely rare, but they can happen after a cascading failure in which something causes some generating stations to trip, redirecting load onto the remaining stations which can't handle it causing them to trip in turn. stories.title_en: Software is breaking down at a systemic level

comments.author: doug_durham
comments.text: This narrative isn't consistent with reality.  Cloud computing is much older than 10 years ago.  We were doing production grade cloud computing over 16 years ago.  The OSS revolution dates to the late 90's.  The author seems to think that SWE was in a golden age 10 years ago.  Sorry, but it's about the same. We have the same problems in SWE as we had 40 years ago.  The scale and ambition of the problems we are solving have increased as compute capabilities have increased.

comments.author: CharlieDigital
comments.text:
It doesn't have to be this way.
AI is great at following patterns.  AI is great at writing tests.  AI is great at doing work that humans would consider drudgery and then applying "enough" judgement to it.
The problem is that most software teams and most engineers are very, very bad at the thing that AI needs to succeed: technical writing.  Documenting the patterns, the rules, the heuristics, the SOP, the judgement; developers could barely be bothered to write comments before (which in the AI age are free, infrastructure-less memory that is always "line-of-sight" for the agent and can be used to enrich with keywords).
It's not that AI is the problem, it's that we humans are good at resolving these constraints in the real world at a human pace.  AI makes that pace impossible for a human to keep up as a trailing activity.  Rather teams need to invest more in technical writing and producing the corpus that AI relies on to learn the operational constraints and rules.

comments.author: illuminator83
comments.text:
Software is not really being more broken today than it was 10 or 20 years ago. It actually has gotten better.
I've seen the codebase of a dozen companies and worked with hundreds of peers.
There is plenty of horrific bugs and bad software outside. The reasons are plentiful too and include everything like budget constraints, management failures and engineering skill issues.
Today, the average code that even a product manager or junior engineer submits is actually excellent overall - if your processes, harness and CI etc are well designed. It is actually super easy to author software well now. Whether you build something that is actually needed and is tasteful is another matter.
99% of the security vulnerabilities being found and exploited today were created by people. Cutting most of them out of the technical details is actually good.

comments.author: rglover
comments.text:
Imo:
the way we make software is breaking down at a systemic level
.
The harsh reality is that some people/systems are adapting just fine to the new way of doing things, others are making a mess of things by rushing via vibe coding and not checking the work (either by choice or by circumstance at work). The results won't be (and shouldn't be expected to be) linear.
The 2010s brought on a very groupthinky dynamic to software dev. This led to a culture where the majority of developers just ask "what is everyone else doing." Now that we're past the blog era of development, that shared reality appears to be breaking down. Now the answer really is "whatever makes sense for/to you," but I think (anecdotally) that's freaking a lot of people and teams out.
For the first time in a long time, a "best practice" doesn't really exist.

comments.author: ljm
comments.text:
Software wasn't exactly hard 12 years ago either, the barriers to entry were being lowered at a rapid pace. 2014 was the dawn of the software bootcamp where JS became more and more pronounced in web architecture.
I feel this piece is either more alarmist than it deserves to be, or it is late to the party.
It uses various incidents in 2026 to prove a point while dismissing those that did take place in the decade or so previous. For example, heartbleed, the log4j RCE, Rails' mass assignment DOS, Cloudflare updating a WAF rule and breaking the internet, Atlassian deleting almost 1000 of its customers' accounts and data, the Ashley Madison breach, Crowdstrike bricking their customers computers, Okta getting owned multiple times, etc.
My own point is that software became like this when we started becoming pragmatic. Nothing to do with AI or management really, we just realised, especially with web tech, that you can release something
and then
fix it. In the old age of getting CDs or floppies printed and distributed, that was not even remotely feasible. A similar incident in the 90s would involve a product recall or a way to get updated media from a retailer with the fix. Very expensive.
